questions.title: WFA-M1 · Fundamental qualitative characteristics
questions.promptMarkdown: Under the IASB Conceptual Framework (Chapter 1), which pair represents the two **fundamental** qualitative characteristics of useful financial information?
hints: Distinguish fundamental qualities from the four enhancing qualities.
Information must both matter to decisions and accurately depict economic substance.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Relevance** and **faithful representation** are the two fundamental qualitative characteristics; comparability, verifiability, timeliness, and understandability are *enhancing* characteristics.
questions.pitfall: Confusing enhancing characteristics (comparability/verifiability) with fundamental characteristics.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M2 · Asset recognition criteria on the SFP
questions.promptMarkdown: Nordic Design AS spends £40,000 training its sales staff on a new CRM system. How should this £40,000 expenditure be treated in the financial statements?
options: Capitalised as an intangible non-current asset and amortised over 5 years
Recognised immediately as an expense in the income statement because the firm lacks legal control over staff remaining
Recorded directly as a deduction from share capital without passing through profit
Held in current assets as prepaid employee goodwill
hints: Check the control test for an asset in Chapter 2.
Employees can resign, so future economic benefits from general training are not controlled by the entity.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Because the business cannot **control** employees' future service, staff training fails the asset recognition test and is expensed immediately in the income statement.
questions.pitfall: Capitalising internally incurred staff training or marketing spend as an intangible asset.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M3 · Double-entry effect of credit purchase settlement
questions.promptMarkdown: When a business pays £12,000 from its bank account to settle an existing trade payable (with no settlement discount), what is the double-entry effect?
options: Debit Trade payables £12,000; Credit Cash at bank £12,000 (equity unchanged)
Debit Cash at bank £12,000; Credit Trade payables £12,000 (equity unchanged)
Debit Purchases expense £12,000; Credit Cash at bank £12,000 (equity decreases)
Debit Trade payables £12,000; Credit Retained earnings £12,000 (equity increases)
hints: Decreasing a liability is a Debit; decreasing an asset is a Credit.
Was any revenue earned or new expense incurred at the moment of cash settlement?
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Paying a supplier reduces the liability **Trade payables** (**Debit £12,000**) and reduces the asset **Cash at bank** (**Credit £12,000**). Total assets and total liabilities fall equally; profit and equity are unaffected.
questions.pitfall: Treating supplier cash payment as an expense at settlement rather than when goods/services were incurred.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M4 · Accrued expense adjustment error
questions.promptMarkdown: If an accountant forgets to record £8,500 of accrued electricity expense at year-end, what is the effect on the year-end financial statements?
options: Profit is understated by £8,500 and current liabilities are overstated by £8,500
Profit is overstated by £8,500 and current liabilities are understated by £8,500
Profit is overstated by £8,500 and cash is overstated by £8,500
Assets are overstated by £8,500 and liabilities are unaffected
hints: Write the missing entry: Dr Electricity expense £8,500, Cr Accruals (current liability) £8,500.
Omitting an expense makes profit too high; omitting the accrual makes liabilities too low.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Omitting an accrued expense leaves expenses £8,500 too low (**profit & equity overstated by £8,500**) and omits the current liability (**current liabilities understated by £8,500**). Cash is unaffected.
questions.pitfall: Assuming accrued expenses affect the year-end cash balance.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M5 · Working capital impact on operating cash flow
questions.promptMarkdown: During 2026, operating profit is £90,000, depreciation is £18,000, inventories increased by £11,000, and trade payables increased by £7,000 (no other working capital items). Cash generated from operations is:
hints: Add back non-cash depreciation to operating profit.
An inventory build-up absorbs cash (−£11,000), whereas higher trade payables conserve cash (+£7,000).
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.pitfall: Flipping the signs on working capital changes (adding inventory increase or subtracting payable increase).

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M6 · Relevant cost of inventory already in stock
questions.promptMarkdown: A firm holds 400 kg of Specialty Alloy bought last year for £15/kg (historic cost £6,000). If not used on a one-off contract, it would be sold immediately as scrap for £9/kg; the alloy has no other use in the business. What is the relevant cost of using the 400 kg on the contract?
options: £0, because the alloy is already paid for
hints: Sunk purchase cost (£15/kg) is always irrelevant.
Ask what cash inflow the firm sacrifices by using the material instead of scrapping it.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: The historic £6,000 is sunk. Using the alloy sacrifices £9/kg in immediate scrap proceeds, so the relevant opportunity cost is $400 \times £9 = \mathbf{£3,600}$.
questions.pitfall: Treating existing material as free (£0) and ignoring its forgone scrap proceeds.

questions.title: WFA-M7 · Operating gearing and profit sensitivity
questions.promptMarkdown: Company H has high fixed costs and low variable cost per unit; Company L has low fixed costs and high variable cost per unit. At the same current sales volume and operating profit, if sales volume rises by 15%:
options: Company L's operating profit will increase by a larger percentage than Company H's
Company H's operating profit will increase by a larger percentage because its contribution margin ratio is higher
Both companies will experience the exact same 15% increase in operating profit
Company H has a lower break-even point when demand falls
hints: Recall operating gearing = Contribution / Operating profit.
High fixed costs with equal profit imply a larger total contribution, magnifying volume swings.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Company H has higher **operating gearing**: each extra unit sold generates a higher contribution while fixed costs stay constant, so profit rises (and falls) by a larger percentage than at Company L.
questions.pitfall: Mixing up operating gearing risk on the downside with profit sensitivity on the upside.

questions.title: WFA-M8 · Traditional volume-based costing vs ABC cross-subsidisation
questions.promptMarkdown: When a multi-product factory switches from a single direct-labour-hour (DLH) overhead rate to Activity-Based Costing (ABC), low-volume complex batch products typically show:
options: A lower unit cost under ABC because they consume fewer total labour hours
A higher unit cost under ABC because batch-level set-up and inspection costs are spread over fewer units
Unchanged unit cost, because total factory overhead is identical
Zero indirect cost, because ABC only traces direct materials
hints: Traditional DLH allocates set-up/inspection pools in proportion to volume.
Small complex batches trigger disproportionate set-ups per unit produced.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Traditional volume-based rates **under-cost** low-volume complex products and **over-cost** high-volume standard products; ABC assigns batch-level set-ups/inspections accurately, raising the reported unit cost of small complex batches.
questions.pitfall: Assuming fewer total DLHs means complex small batches become cheaper under ABC.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M9 · Mutually exclusive projects: NPV vs IRR
questions.promptMarkdown: Projects X (initial outlay £50,000, IRR 22%, NPV +£14,000) and Y (initial outlay £200,000, IRR 17%, NPV +£29,000) are mutually exclusive at a 10% cost of capital with no capital rationing. To maximise shareholder wealth, the firm should:
options: Accept Project X because 22% IRR exceeds 17% IRR
Accept Project Y because it generates the higher positive Net Present Value (+£29,000)
Accept both X and Y because both have positive NPVs
Reject both until their IRRs are equal
hints: IRR is a percentage rate and ignores project scale.
Which metric directly measures absolute shareholder wealth added in today's pounds?
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: **NPV** directly measures absolute wealth creation in present-value monetary terms (+£29,000 vs +£14,000). For mutually exclusive projects, IRR suffers from the **scale problem**.
questions.pitfall: Ranking mutually exclusive projects of different sizes by IRR percentage instead of NPV.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M10 · Working capital in NPV cash-flow schedules
questions.promptMarkdown: A 4-year project requires £25,000 of net working capital at $t = 0$, maintained throughout Years 1–4 and fully recovered at the end of Year 4 ($t = 4$) at a 10% discount rate. What is the net effect of working capital on the project's **NPV**?
options: £0, because −£25,000 at t=0 and +£25,000 at t=4 cancel out
Negative (−£7,924.66), because the t=4 recovery is discounted while the t=0 outflow is not
Negative (−£25,000), because working capital release is an accounting entry rather than cash
Positive (+£17,075.34), because working capital recovery adds to Year 4 profit
hints: Time value of money means tying up cash for 4 years carries an opportunity cost.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: In undiscounted terms $-25,000 + 25,000 = 0$, but in present value $-25,000 + 25,000 / 1.10^4 = -25,000 + 17,075.34 = \mathbf{-£7,924.66}$. Tying up working capital reduces NPV by the lost time value.
questions.pitfall: Omitting the t=4 working capital release OR claiming t=0 and t=4 cancel in PV terms.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-E1 · Nordic Craft Ltd · FIFO, Accruals, Income Statement & Equity (45 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
Complete **Exercise 1 (45 points)** under WISEflow FLOWmulti rules (2 decimals / ±2% rounding margin; use minus sign for negatives).

**Data for Nordic Craft Ltd (Year ended 31 December 2026):**
- **Sales revenue:** £420,000 (all credit sales). Irrecoverable receivables written off during 2026: **£4,000**.
- **Inventory batches (FIFO cost flow):**
  - 1 Jan opening inventory: `200 units @ £40 = £8,000`
  - 14 Apr purchase: `500 units @ £44 = £22,000`
  - 9 Oct purchase: `400 units @ £50 = £20,000`
  - Total units sold during 2026: **800 units**.
- **Operating costs & year-end adjustments:**
  - Cash wages paid in 2026: **£140,000**; unpaid December wages accrued at year-end: **£6,000**.
  - Cash rent paid in 2026: **£48,000**, which includes **£8,000** prepaid for Jan–Feb 2027.
  - Workshop equipment cost **£120,000**, residual value **£20,000**, useful life **5 years** (straight-line depreciation).
  - Other cash operating expenses: **£55,000** · Loan interest expense: **£10,000**.
- **Equity roll-forward:** Opening total equity (1 Jan 2026) = **£250,000**; cash dividends paid in 2026 = **£30,000** (no new share issues).

**Statement 1a:** Under rising unit purchase prices, FIFO reports a higher closing inventory value and higher profit than AVCO.
**Statement 1b:** Paying a cash dividend to shareholders is recorded as an operating expense in the income statement.
**Statement 1c:** Prepaid rent at year-end is classified as a current asset on the Statement of Financial Position.

Add accrued wages (+£6,000), deduct prepaid rent (−£8,000), deduct straight-line depreciation ((120,000 − 20,000)/5 = £20,000) and bad debts (£4,000). Dividends reduce Retained Earnings directly, not Net Profit.
rubricChecks: Computed FIFO closing inventory (£15,000) and COGS (£35,000)

questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFA-E1 (45 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(dividends are an appropriation of retained earnings, not an expense)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **FIFO Inventory & Gross Profit:**
   - Available goods $= 8,000 + 22,000 + 20,000 = £50,000$ ($1,100$ units). Closing units $= 1,100 - 800 = 300$ units from 9 Oct batch $@ £50 = \mathbf{£15,000}$.
   - $\text{COGS} = 50,000 - 15,000 = \mathbf{£35,000}$ *(check: $200(40) + 500(44) + 100(50) = 8,000 + 22,000 + 5,000 = 35,000$)*.
   - $\text{Gross Profit} = 420,000 - 35,000 = \mathbf{£385,000}$.
3. **Operating & Net Profit:**
   - Wages expense $= 140,000 + 6,000 = \mathbf{£146,000}$ · Rent expense $= 48,000 - 8,000 = \mathbf{£40,000}$ · Depreciation $= (120,000 - 20,000)/5 = \mathbf{£20,000}$.
   - Total operating expenses $= 146,000 + 40,000 + 20,000 + 4,000 + 55,000 = £265,000 \implies \text{Operating Profit} = 385,000 - 265,000 = \mathbf{£120,000}$.
   - $\text{Net Profit} = 120,000 - 10,000 = \mathbf{£110,000}$.
4. **Closing Equity:** $250,000 + 110,000 - 30,000 = \mathbf{£330,000}$.
questions.pitfall: Subtracting dividends inside Net Profit, or forgetting to subtract residual value (£20,000) in straight-line depreciation.

pacing.rationale: 45-point WISEflow FLOWmulti exercise (45m exam par at 1 pt = 1 min; ±2% rounding margin).

questions.title: WFA-E2 · Bergen Marine Ltd · Indirect Statement of Cash Flows (35 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
Complete **Exercise 2 (35 points)** for **Bergen Marine Ltd** (all figures in **£m**; enter numbers only, using a minus sign e.g. `-57` for net outflows).

**Summary Data for 2026 (£m):**
- **Operating profit (EBIT):** `84` (after charging depreciation of `26` and a **loss on disposal** of equipment of `5`).
- The disposed equipment had a carrying amount (NBV) of `18` and was sold for **`13` cash**.
- **Property, Plant & Equipment (carrying amount / NBV):** Opening `210` · Closing `236` (all additions were paid in cash).
- **Working capital balances (Opening → Closing):**
  - Inventories: `30 → 39`
  - Trade receivables: `45 → 41`
  - Trade payables: `28 → 22`
- **Interest, Tax & Financing:** Interest paid in cash = `8`. Income statement tax charge = `16`; Tax payable on SFP went from Opening `14` to Closing `11`. New long-term bank loan raised = `20`; Cash dividends paid (classified under **Financing activities** here) = `12`.
- **Opening cash / bank balance (1 Jan 2026):** Bank overdraft of **`-10`**.

**Statement 1a:** A non-cash loss on disposal of non-current assets is added back to operating profit when reconciling to cash generated from operations, while the actual sale proceeds appear under investing activities.
**Statement 1b:** Making a bonus issue of shares (capitalising reserves) generates a financing cash inflow.
**Statement 1c:** Profitable rapidly growing firms can experience negative operating cash flow if inventory and receivable expansion exceeds operating cash generation.

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Disposal loss add-back & investing proceeds
1b. Bonus share issue creates financing cash inflow
1c. Profitable growth can cause negative operating cash flow (overtrading)
Cash Generated from Operations (before interest & tax)
Cash Tax Paid during 2026 (enter positive magnitude 19 or -19)
Net Cash from Operating Activities (after interest 8 & tax paid)
Cash Paid for PPE Additions (magnitude 70 or -70)
Net Cash from Investing Activities (use minus sign)
Net Cash from Financing Activities
Closing Cash Balance at 31 Dec 2026

hints: Cash generated = Operating profit (84) + Depreciation (26) + Disposal loss (5) − ΔInventory (9) + ΔReceivables decrease (4) − ΔPayables decrease (6).
Roll forward PPE NBV: Opening (210) + Additions − Disposal NBV (18) − Depreciation (26) = Closing (236) ⇒ Additions = 70. Net investing = −70 + 13 disposal cash = −57.
rubricChecks: Added back both depreciation (26) and loss on disposal (5) in Operating cash
Reconciled Tax Paid (14 + 16 − 11 = 19) and PPE Additions (70) via roll-forward
Combined Opening Overdraft (−10) + Net Change (+28) = +18 Closing Cash
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFA-E2 (35 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(a bonus issue transfers reserves to share capital with zero cash flow)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Operating Activities (£m):**
   - $\text{Cash generated} = 84 + 26 + 5 - (39 - 30) + (45 - 41) - (28 - 22) = 115 - 9 + 4 - 6 = \mathbf{104}$.
   - $\text{Tax paid} = 14 + 16 - 11 = \mathbf{19}$.
   - $\text{Net cash from operating activities} = 104 - 8 - 19 = \mathbf{77}$.
3. **Investing & Financing Activities (£m):**
   - $\text{PPE Additions} = 236 - 210 + 18 + 26 = \mathbf{70} \implies \text{Net investing cash flow} = -70 + 13 = \mathbf{-57}$.
   - $\text{Net financing cash flow} = +20\text{ (loan)} - 12\text{ (dividends)} = \mathbf{+8}$.
4. **Closing Cash:** Net change $= 77 - 57 + 8 = +28 \implies -10 + 28 = \mathbf{+18\text{ (£m)}}$.
questions.pitfall: Subtracting disposal loss instead of adding it back, or forgetting disposal NBV (18) and depreciation (26) when solving for PPE additions.

questions.title: WFA-E3 · Oslo Mobility · Break-Even, Margin of Safety & Scarce Machine Hours (30 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
Complete **Exercise 3 (30 points)** for **Oslo Mobility Ltd**.

**Part A — Single-Product CVP (Commuter e-bike):**
- Selling price = **£500/unit** · Variable cost = **£300/unit** · Monthly fixed costs = **£120,000**.
- Budgeted monthly sales volume = **800 units**.

**Part B — Two-Product Limiting Factor Decision:**
Next quarter, Oslo Mobility can also sell a **Cargo** model (Selling price **£750**, Variable cost **£450**, max monthly demand **300 units**) alongside **Commuter** (max monthly demand **600 units**). Specialised CNC machine capacity is capped at **2,100 machine hours (MH)** per month (Fixed costs remain **£120,000**):
- **Commuter:** requires **2.5 MH** per unit.
- **Cargo:** requires **5.0 MH** per unit.

**Statement 1a:** Margin of safety (%) measures the percentage by which budgeted sales can fall before the business incurs an operating loss.
**Statement 1b:** When machine hours are the single scarce limiting factor, products should be ranked by highest contribution per unit of output.
**Statement 1c:** An increase in the income tax rate raises the pre-tax sales volume required to earn a specified **after-tax** target profit.

Rank by CM per scarce machine hour: Commuter = £200 / 2.5 MH = £80/MH vs Cargo = £300 / 5.0 MH = £60/MH. Fulfil Commuter's 600-unit demand first!
rubricChecks: Calculated BEP (600 units), MOS (25%), and target-profit volume (950 units)

questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFA-E3 (30 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(rank by contribution **per unit of the scarce resource**, £/MH)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Part A (CVP):**
   - $\text{BEP} = 120,000 / (500 - 300) = \mathbf{600\text{ units}}$.
   - $\text{Margin of Safety \%} = (800 - 600)/800 \times 100 = \mathbf{25\%}$.
   - $\text{Target units} = (120,000 + 70,000)/200 = \mathbf{950\text{ units}}$.
3. **Part B (Scarce Machine Hours):**
   - Commuter: $£200 / 2.5\text{ MH} = \mathbf{£80/\text{MH}}$ (Rank 1) · Cargo: $£300 / 5.0\text{ MH} = £60/\text{MH}$ (Rank 2).
   - Produce max **600 Commuter** units ($600 \times 2.5 = 1,500\text{ MH}$). Remaining capacity $= 2,100 - 1,500 = 600\text{ MH} \implies 600 / 5.0 = \mathbf{120\text{ Cargo units}}$.
   - $\text{Max Operating Profit} = 600(200) + 120(300) - 120,000 = 120,000 + 36,000 - 120,000 = \mathbf{£36,000}$.
questions.pitfall: Dividing Margin of Safety by BEP (600) instead of budgeted sales (800), or prioritising Cargo because £300 > £200 per unit.

questions.title: WFA-E4 · Fjord Tech · NPV, Working Capital Recovery, Payback & ARR (30 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
Complete **Exercise 4 (30 points)** for **Fjord Tech AS** (Cost of capital $r = 10\%$).

**Project Data:**
- **Equipment outlay ($t = 0$):** £160,000 · Expected residual (disposal) value at $t = 4$: **£20,000** (4-year life, straight-line depreciation).
- **Working capital:** **£20,000** required immediately at $t = 0$, fully recovered in cash at the end of Year 4 ($t = 4$).
- **Annual net operating cash inflows** (before depreciation):
  - $t = 1$: **£55,000** · $t = 2$: **£65,000** · $t = 3$: **£60,000** · $t = 4$: **£50,000**.
- *(10% discount factors if needed: $t=1: 0.9091$, $t=2: 0.8264$, $t=3: 0.7513$, $t=4: 0.6830$.)*

**Statement 1a:** Depreciation is a non-cash expense and must not be deducted from cash flows in an NPV schedule, though it reduces accounting profit in ARR.
**Statement 1b:** Financing interest charges on loans used to fund the project should be subtracted as an annual cash outflow in the project's cash-flow line before discounting at the cost of capital.
**Statement 1c:** Accounting Rate of Return (ARR) ignores the timing of cash flows within the project's life.

questions.title: WFB-M10 · Real vs nominal cash flows and discount rates
questions.promptMarkdown: When evaluating capital projects in the presence of general inflation, the golden consistency rule requires:
options: Discounting nominal (money) cash flows at the real cost of capital
Discounting real cash flows at the nominal (money) cost of capital
Either discounting nominal cash flows at the nominal rate OR real cash flows at the real rate (both give the exact same NPV)
Ignoring inflation completely because sales prices and costs never change
hints: Recall Fisher's relation $(1 + m) = (1 + r)(1 + i)$.
Match nominal with nominal, or real with real — never mix them!

Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately

questions.title: WFB-E1 · Viken Retail · Reducing-Balance Depreciation, Asset Disposal & Doubtful Debts (40 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
Complete **Exercise 1 (40 points)** for **Viken Retail AS** (Year ended 31 December 2026).

**1. Delivery Fleet & 1 January Transactions:**
- At 1 Jan 2026 (before transactions), the fleet had original cost **£200,000** and accumulated depreciation **£72,000** (Opening NBV = **£128,000**).
- On **1 Jan 2026**, Viken sold an older van (original cost **£50,000**, accumulated depreciation **£28,000**) for **£17,000 cash**, and immediately purchased a replacement van for **£54,000 cash**.
- Viken depreciates all vehicles at **25% per annum reducing-balance** on year-end carrying amount prior to 2026 depreciation.

**2. Trade Receivables & Allowance for Doubtful Debts:**
- Gross trade receivables at 31 Dec 2026 (before write-offs) = **£95,000**; Opening allowance for doubtful debts (1 Jan) = **£2,600**.
- At 31 Dec, a bankrupt customer owing **£5,000** is written off as irrecoverable, and the closing allowance is set at **4%** of remaining trade receivables.

**3. Draft Profit:** Draft operating profit **before** recording (i) the van disposal gain/loss, (ii) 2026 depreciation, and (iii) 2026 bad & doubtful debt charges was **£145,000**.

**Statement 1a:** Changing depreciation method purely to hit a management bonus target violates faithful representation unless the pattern of economic benefit consumption genuinely changed.
**Statement 1b:** Accumulated depreciation represents a ring-fenced cash fund set aside in the bank to buy replacement machinery.
**Statement 1c:** Increasing the allowance for doubtful debts reduces both reported profit and net current assets.

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Depreciation method reflects economic consumption, not bonus smoothing
1b. Accumulated depreciation is a cash replacement fund
1c. Higher doubtful-debt allowance lowers profit and net current assets

hints: Disposed van NBV = £50,000 − £28,000 = £22,000; sold for £17,000 ⇒ −£5,000 loss. Active fleet NBV before 2026 depreciation = (£128,000 − £22,000) + £54,000 = £160,000.

Write off £5,000 first so remaining receivables = £90,000. Closing allowance = 4% × £90,000 = £3,600 (only the £1,000 increase over £2,600 opening allowance is an extra expense alongside the £5,000 write-off!).
rubricChecks: Calculated van disposal loss (−£5,000), 2026 depreciation (£40,000), and closing NBV (£120,000)

questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFB-E1 (40 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(depreciation is book cost allocation, not cash)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Fleet Disposal & Depreciation:**
   - Disposed NBV $= 50,000 - 28,000 = £22,000 \implies \text{Disposal result} = 17,000 - 22,000 = \mathbf{-£5,000}$ (loss).
   - Depreciable base $= (128,000 - 22,000) + 54,000 = £160,000 \implies \text{2026 Depreciation} = 0.25 \times 160,000 = \mathbf{£40,000}$.
   - Closing fleet NBV $= 160,000 - 40,000 = \mathbf{£120,000}$.
3. **Receivables & Operating Profit:**
   - Remaining gross receivables $= 95,000 - 5,000 = £90,000 \implies \text{Closing allowance} = 0.04 \times 90,000 = \mathbf{£3,600}$.
   - Income statement charge $= £5,000\text{ (write-off)} + (£3,600 - £2,600)\text{ (Δallowance)} = \mathbf{£6,000}$.
   - Net SFP receivables $= 90,000 - 3,600 = \mathbf{£86,400}$.
   - Adjusted Operating Profit $= 145,000 - 5,000 - 40,000 - 6,000 = \mathbf{£94,000}$.
questions.pitfall: Expensing the entire £3,600 closing allowance instead of the £1,000 movement above £2,600 opening allowance.

questions.title: WFB-E2 · Stavanger Engineering · Relevant Costing & Minimum Contract Price (35 pts)

**Statement 1b:** Past R&D/feasibility costs become relevant if the contract successfully goes ahead and recovers them.
**Statement 1c:** Relevant cost-based minimum pricing defines a short-run floor for one-off spare/constrained decisions, whereas long-run survival requires covering full costs.

questions.title: WFC-M1 · Shareholder wealth maximisation vs short-term profit
questions.promptMarkdown: Why does modern corporate finance assume **shareholder wealth maximisation** rather than **short-term accounting profit maximisation** as the primary financial objective?

Accounting profit is illegal to report in annual accounts
Shareholder wealth ignores future cash flows beyond 12 months
Short-term profit always equals net cash flow
hints: Consider how slashing R&D, maintenance, or training affects this year's profit vs future value.
Wealth (market value) discounts expected future cash flows at a risk-adjusted rate.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Short-term profit can be inflated by cutting value-creating R&D/maintenance and ignores **risk** and the **time value of money**; shareholder wealth incorporates risk-adjusted lifetime cash flows.

The company's share price rises above book equity

Only an external acquisition transaction establishes an objective price for goodwill.

Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately

questions.title: WFC-M4 · AVCO vs FIFO cost of sales
questions.promptMarkdown: On 1 May a store has 100 units @ £10 (£1,000). On 10 May it buys 100 units @ £16 (£1,600). On 20 May it sells 120 units. Under **periodic weighted-average cost (AVCO)**, Cost of Sales is:

questions.title: WFC-E1 · Trondheim BioLabs · Equity Roll-Forward & Full Cash-Flow Reconciliation (40 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
Complete **Exercise 1 (40 points)** for **Trondheim BioLabs AS** (all figures in **£000**; use minus sign for negatives).

**1. Equity & Income Data (£000):**
- Opening Total Equity (1 Jan 2026) = `400` · Closing Total Equity (31 Dec 2026) = `515`.
- During 2026, Trondheim issued new shares for **`50` cash** and paid cash dividends of **`25`** (classified under **Financing activities**). No revaluations occurred.
- Income statement includes Loan Interest Expense = `12` (paid in cash) and Tax Expense = `18` (actual cash tax paid in 2026 = **`20`**).

**2. Operating, Investing & Financing Details (£000):**
- Operating profit is stated after charging Depreciation of **`32`** and crediting a **Gain on disposal** of lab equipment of **`6`** (the equipment was sold for **`16` cash**).
- Cash paid to purchase new lab equipment = **`85`** · Bank loan principal repaid = **`30`**.
- Working capital (Opening → Closing): Inventories `50 → 44` · Trade receivables `60 → 75` · Trade payables `35 → 42`.
- Opening Cash at Bank (1 Jan 2026) = **`14`**.

**Statement 1a:** An accounting **gain** on disposal of equipment must be **deducted** from operating profit in the indirect cash-flow reconciliation so it is not double-counted alongside investing sale proceeds.
**Statement 1b:** Repaying principal on a bank loan reduces Net Profit on the income statement.
**Statement 1c:** If Opening Equity + New Shares + Net Profit − Dividends = Closing Equity, Net Profit can be deduced directly from SFP equity movements.

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Deduct disposal gain from operating profit in indirect cash flows
1b. Loan principal repayment is an income statement expense
1c. Clean-surplus equity roll-forward deduces Net Profit
2026 Net Profit (after interest & tax)
2026 Operating Profit (EBIT)
Cash Generated from Operations (before interest & tax)
Net Cash from Operating Activities (after interest 12 & tax paid 20)
Net Cash from Investing Activities (use minus sign)
Net Cash from Financing Activities (use minus sign)
Closing Cash Balance at 31 Dec 2026

hints: First solve Equity roll-forward: 400 + 50 + Net Profit − 25 = 515 ⇒ Net Profit = 90. Add back interest (12) and tax charge (18) to reach EBIT = 120.
Cash generated = 120 + 32 (depr) − 6 (disposal gain!) + 6 (inv decrease) − 15 (AR increase) + 7 (AP increase) = 144. Deduct cash interest (12) and cash tax paid (20), NOT tax expense (18)!
rubricChecks: Deduced Net Profit (90) and Operating Profit EBIT (120) from equity roll-forward
Subtracted non-cash disposal gain (−6) and adjusted WC to reach 144 cash generated & 112 net operating
Computed Investing (−69), Financing (−5), and Closing Cash (52)
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFC-E1 (40 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(only interest is an expense; principal repayment reduces Cash and Loan Liability)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Profit Deduction (£000):** $400 + 50 + \text{NP} - 25 = 515 \implies \text{NP} = \mathbf{90}$. $\text{EBIT} = 90 + 12 + 18 = \mathbf{120}$.
3. **Cash Flows (£000):**
   - $\text{Cash generated} = 120 + 32 - 6 + (50 - 44) - (75 - 60) + (42 - 35) = 146 + 6 - 15 + 7 = \mathbf{144}$.
   - $\text{Net operating cash} = 144 - 12 - 20 = \mathbf{112}$.
   - $\text{Net investing cash} = -85 + 16 = \mathbf{-69}$.
   - $\text{Net financing cash} = +50 - 30 - 25 = \mathbf{-5}$.
   - $\text{Closing cash} = 14 + (112 - 69 - 5) = 14 + 38 = \mathbf{52}$.
questions.pitfall: Adding the £6k disposal gain instead of subtracting it, or subtracting £18k tax expense instead of £20k cash tax paid.

questions.title: WFC-E2 · Aurora Ski Gear · Multi-Product Break-Even, Segment Continuation & Gearing (35 pts)

| Line | Current Units | Selling Price | Variable Cost/u | Avoidable Line Fixed Cost | Apportioned HQ Fixed Cost |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Alpine (60%)** | 2,400 | £300 | £180 | £70,000 | £50,000 |
| **Nordic (40%)** | 1,600 | £200 | £130 | £80,000 | £50,000 |
| **Company Total** | **4,000** | — | — | **£150,000** | **£100,000** *(Total FC = £250,000)* |

At 1,600 units, Nordic shows an accounting loss of $£112,000 - £80,000 - £50,000 = -£18,000$. Management asks whether to **drop Nordic** (assuming **zero** HQ fixed cost savings and zero effect on Alpine demand).

**Statement 1a:** Multi-product break-even analysis assumes a constant sales mix; shifting the mix toward the higher-contribution product lowers the total break-even unit volume.
**Statement 1b:** Because Nordic reports a −£18,000 bottom-line loss after HQ apportionment, dropping Nordic will raise total company profit by +£18,000.
**Statement 1c:** Degree of operating gearing (`Total Contribution / Operating Profit`) predicts the percentage change in operating profit from a 1% change in volume (at constant mix).

1b. Dropping Nordic increases company profit by +£18,000
1c. Operating gearing ratio measures profit elasticity to volume

Nordic earns £112,000 contribution and saves only £80,000 avoidable fixed cost if closed — losing +£32,000 net contribution toward HQ! Use a minus sign (−32000).

questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFC-E2 (35 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(company profit falls by £32,000)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Multi-Product Break-Even:**
   - $\text{Weighted CM} = 0.6(120) + 0.4(70) = \mathbf{£100/\text{unit}}$.
   - $\text{Total BEP} = 250,000 / 100 = \mathbf{2,500\text{ units}}$ (`60% × 2,500 =` **1,500 Alpine** + `1,000 Nordic`).
3. **Keep-or-Drop & Operating Gearing:**
   - Current Contribution $= 4,000 \times 100 = £400,000 \implies \text{Operating Profit} = 400,000 - 250,000 = \mathbf{£150,000}$.
   - Dropping Nordic loses $£112,000$ contribution while saving only $£80,000$ avoidable fixed cost $\implies \Delta\text{Profit} = \mathbf{-£32,000}$ *(new profit $= £118,000$)*.
